issues.legal_issue: A family qualifies as descendants of a former Ruling Chief only if its ancestor possessed the attributes of sovereignty.
material_facts: The claimants sought a maintenance grant on the basis that their ancestors were former Ruling Chiefs.
The ancestors received hereditary offices and revenue rights, and later a jagir over several villages, in recognition of services to the Peshwas.
The grants and subsequent records described the ancestors as officials, watandars or jagirdars; the evidence did not establish that they exercised sovereign powers over the jagir.
The State Government found that the ancestors had not been Ruling Chiefs, and the Supreme Court found no jurisdictional error or incorrect determination of the basic facts in that decision.
issues.conclusion: The ancestors were not Ruling Chiefs, so the claimants were not entitled to a grant under section 5(3)(ii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Revocation of Land Revenue Exemptions Act, 1948; the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: The expression “Ruling Chief,” which is not defined in the Act, bears its common meaning: a person endowed with the content and attributes of sovereignty. Sovereignty is the supreme power governing the body politic, regardless of the form of government. Section 5(3)(ii) permits a grant for the suitable maintenance of a family descended from a former Ruling Chief. In the earlier decision in Sardar Govindrao v. State of Madhya Pradesh, the Court held that the word “may” in section 5(3) is compulsory once the statutory condition precedent exists; it does not dispense with proof that the family meets that condition.

predicates.maintenance_grant_claim: A family applied for a grant for its maintenance on the basis that it descended from a former ruler.
predicates.ancestor_lacked_sovereign_attributes: The evidence showed that the ancestor held offices or a jagir but did not possess the attributes of sovereign power.

issues.definition: When a family seeks a maintenance grant based on descent from a former ruler and its ancestor lacked sovereign attributes, the family is not entitled to the grant.

issues.legal_issue: After territorial cession, an inhabitant cannot enforce proprietary rights in municipal courts merely because a treaty or proclamation generally promises to respect existing rights; the claimant must establish that the new sovereign recognized the rights.
material_facts: A treaty governing the territorial transfer provided for respect of existing leases and for new grants concerning rent-free lands, jagirs, perquisites and hereditary claims.
After the transfer, the British Government investigated the estates and their tenures and decided that the zamindars, apart from a specified chief, were to be treated as ordinary British subjects.
The claimants did not prove that the British Government had acknowledged or recognized sovereign rights held by their ancestors.
issues.conclusion: The treaty’s general promise to respect existing rights did not establish enforceable sovereign rights for the claimants, and they failed to prove that the new sovereign had recognized such rights.
issues.legal_principle: On acquisition of territory by conquest, cession or otherwise, an inhabitant may enforce in municipal courts only proprietary rights conferred or recognized by the new sovereign. A general treaty or proclamation promising recognition of existing rights means that the government will recognize rights found to exist after investigation; it does not itself confer enforceable rights on inhabitants. The burden of proving recognition rested on the claimants. The Court relied on Vajesingji Joravarsingji v. Secretary of State for India in Council, Bir Bikram Deo v. Secretary of State for India in Council, and Martand Rao v. Malhar Rao.

predicates.territorial_cession_dispute: A person asserted rights over property in territory transferred to a new sovereign.
predicates.treaty_generally_promised_respect_for_ex: The transfer agreement generally promised to respect rights that existed before the transfer.
predicates.new_sovereign_recognized_claimed_rights: The new sovereign recognized the rights asserted by the claimant after investigating the relevant title or tenure.

issues.definition: In a territorial cession dispute, a general promise to respect existing rights does not make claimed rights enforceable in municipal courts when the new sovereign did not recognize them.
